title: The Man Without a Past
full_review:
A man wakes up with no memory, money or identity in the drolly humanistic tale "The Man Without a Past" (Sony Classics).

After getting off a train at Helsinki, Finland, a man (Markku Peltola) with a suitcase is severely beaten by three thugs and left for dead outside the railroad station.

Coming to in a hospital, his face wrapped in bandages (reminiscent of a scene from "The Invisible Man"), he wanders outside and is temporarily taken in by a poor waterfront family. The people around him live in abandoned freight ship containers, and soon the stoic amnesiac is in one of his own, complete with a discarded jukebox and a scruffy dog, Hannibal, that he must watch in the owner's absence.

An example of the film's abundant deadpan wit is when a neighbor's invitation to dine out means a meal at the nearby soup kitchen. There the Salvation Army band plays hymns as one of their blonde officers (Kati Outinen) catches his eye. Extremely formal courtship follows, holding hands in the storage container -- although she wonders if the laconic stranger could be faking his total amnesia. He, meanwhile, has invited the hymn-playing band to listen to his jukebox tunes and soon has them playing rock, albeit with righteous lyrics, at a genuine gig.

However, after innocent involvement in a bank robbery, his past catches up with him, threatening his newfound, peaceful existence.

Writer-director Ari Kaurismaki observes his characters with a wry eye and a gentle, almost melancholy compassion infused with subtle humor. The amnesiac never loses his dignity, even when asking for hot water in a cafe -- to which he adds a carefully wrapped up, previously used teabag. The sympathetic cashier quickly delivers some free leftovers to his table. Nor is the scene where he confronts his past a disappointment as the characters behave in bittersweet, unexpected ways that will again provoke smiles.

Peltola's Chaplinesque portrayal blends being morose and sympathetic just as the solemn Outinen is quietly hilarious as the poker-faced Salvation Army worker whose one guilty pleasure is playing raucous rock on her headphones at night.

The combination of soulful Finnish visuals, spare dialogue and measured sentimentality leads to a deftly resonant film that stands apart from the many Hollywood films that have used a character with amnesia as a gimmicky plot device.

Except for the trio of thugs who ultimately get their comeuppance, the hardscrabble characters are able to look beyond their own problems and reach out to others in ways that give the film a big heart and a universal appeal.

Hopefully, "The Man Without a Past" will have a future as the film expands across the country.

Subtitles.

Due to brief violence and an off-screen suicide, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
